extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, meta-analysts, health researchers and policy-makers studying publication/dissemination bias
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical evidence for identifying, measuring and interpreting different types of research dissemination bias (publication bias, outcome reporting bias, etc.) mainly in clinical trials and cohorts, with methodological recommendations for systematic reviewers and meta-analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of study results by statistical significance (p < 0.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most objective method would be to classify quantitative results as statistically significant (p < 0.05) or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible use objective classification (p<0.05). Other methods used to classify study results as important or not may introduce bias because they are inevitably subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funnel plot asymmetry / Peters et al. test
rubrics_metrics.description: Funnel plot asymmetry test using the method of Peters et al.; example p-values reported: p = 0.178 (inception), p = 0.262 (regulatory), p = 0.233 (abstract), p = 0.942 (manuscript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-significant funnel plot asymmetry does not necessarily rule out publication/reporting bias; interpret with caution and consider other evidence (e.g., missing reports of association between publication and results in abstracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of dissemination bias (dimensions to evaluate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of research dissemination bias include outcome reporting bias, time lag publication bias, grey literature bias, language bias, citation bias, duplicate or multiple publication bias, place of publication bias, database bias, country bias and media attention bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviews should consider and, where possible, assess multiple types of dissemination bias rather than only classical 'publication bias'. The chapter reviews empirical evidence for each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome reporting bias occurs when studies with multiple outcomes report only some of the outcomes measured and the selection of an outcome for reporting is associated with the statistical significance or importance of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also termed 'within-study reporting bias' to distinguish it from selective non-reporting of a whole study; focus is on incomplete reporting within published studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of measured outcomes as prerequisite for selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a large number of measured or calculated outcomes within a study is the prerequisite of selective reporting bias, which is present in almost all research studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: median reported end points per trial often multiple (e.g., median 6, ranges reported). Protocols sometimes specify many more outcomes than appear in publications (e.g., median 20 efficacy outcomes in protocols). A large outcome set increases opportunities for selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of selection producing within-study reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of outcomes to report can be classified into: (1) the selection of outcomes investigated, (2) the selection of methods to measure the selected outcome, and (3) the selection of results of multiple subgroup analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinations of these choices generate many potential results and increase the chance of selectively reporting favourable/significant findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-evidence method: compare protocol-specified outcomes with reported outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The most direct evidence on outcome reporting bias comes from studies that compared outcomes specified in research protocols and those reported in subsequent articles (e.g., Hahn et al., Chan et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence/absence of analysis plans, whether published reports follow the protocol-specified primary outcomes, and quantify discrepancies (examples: primary outcomes changed in 62% (Danish) and 40% (Canadian) cohorts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and identification of incompletely reported outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a published article provided insufficient data for meta-analysis, the outcome was defined as being incompletely reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracking incompletely reported outcomes is important because such outcomes often cannot be included in meta-analyses; reviewers may need to contact trialists but this is time-consuming and often unsuccessful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of individual patient data (IPD) versus published-data meta-analyses to detect selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing meta-analyses based on published data with IPD meta-analyses can reveal missing or selectively reported outcomes (example: McCormack et al. found qualitative divergence for persisting pain outcome when IPD was used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPD may include more trials and outcomes; differences between IPD and published-data pooled estimates indicate potential selective reporting affecting conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort categories for studies of publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies use cohort types such as inception cohorts, regulatory cohorts, abstract cohorts and manuscript cohorts to study publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different cohort types may show different extents of bias (e.g., regulatory cohorts in this review showed greater extent of publication bias), and some cohort selections may themselves be biased (e.g., small numbers or topic-specific cohorts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity assessment in meta-analyses (I2 and p-value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report heterogeneity test statistics (i2 and p value) for pooled estimates; there was statistically significant heterogeneity within some subgroups (e.g., inception, regulatory, abstract cohorts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate sources of heterogeneity (study design, research question, cohort assembly, definitions of study results). Excluding outlying studies may remove heterogeneity (example: Misakian and Bero study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of primary outcomes between protocol and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcomes specified in protocols were different from primary outcomes stated in the corresponding journal articles in a substantial proportion of cases (e.g., 62% Danish cohort, 40% Canadian cohort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check trial protocols vs publications to detect switching of primary outcomes; outcome switching that favours significant results is evidence of selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odds ratios as measures of association between statistical significance and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistically significant outcomes were more likely to be fully reported than non-significant outcomes; example odds ratios: efficacy outcomes OR 2.4 (Danish) and 2.7 (Canadian); harm outcomes ORs larger (e.g., 4.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pooled odds ratios (with 95% CI) to quantify outcome reporting bias; interpret CIs and study contexts (small samples or high uncertainty for some estimates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented reasons for non-reporting of outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors reported reasons for not reporting efficacy and harm outcomes including space constraints (47% and 25%), lack of clinical importance (37% and 75%), and being statistically non-significant (24% and 50%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect authors' stated reasons where possible; these reasons can inform bias assessments but do not substitute for objective protocol vs report comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability of reported results for meta-analysis (proportion usable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of reported results usable in meta-analyses varies; example Bekkering et al. found only 61% of reported results could be used in dose–response meta-analyses of observational studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate proportion of usable results in systematic reviews; lower usability can bias pooled estimates because usable results may be more likely to indicate associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensitivity analyses/imputation to assess impact of missing or non-contributing trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity analysis by imputation of missing within-study results can change pooled estimates substantially (example: Williamson and Gamble showed pooled treatment effect decreased when missing results were imputed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When within-study reporting bias is suspected, conduct sensitivity analyses (e.g., imputation scenarios) to assess robustness of meta-analysis conclusions to missing/unreported outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caution: observational/cohort diversity and confounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Large cohort studies often include highly diverse cases (research questions, designs, other characteristics) which may be associated with both study results and the possibility of publication; adjusted analyses may be conducted but it is generally impossible to exclude confounding impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting pooled associations between results and publication, consider potential confounding (sample size, design, topic, investigator characteristics) and the limits of adjustment in observational cohorts.
